title: Understanding a Canadian Paycheque
subtitle: Your pay stub is not lying to you. It just isn’t explaining itself.

blocks.text: Your pay stub is not lying to you. It just isn’t explaining itself.
You earn a number. A smaller number lands in your account. In between, five or six lines take a bite. Most of us just accept the final number and move on.
That’s fine, until something changes. A raise. A new job. A side gig. Suddenly the math on your stub doesn’t match what you expected, and nobody ever taught you why.
This lesson fixes that. Short version: every deduction on your pay stub has a name, a purpose and a limit. Once you know all three, the stub stops being a mystery.
Know where every dollar of your pay goes, and spot a mistake before it costs you.
blocks.detail: Once you can name each line on your stub, a raise, a new job or a second job stops feeling like a guessing game.
blocks.extra: Section 06 puts all of this year’s rates on one card.

sections.title: The five lines on almost every stub

blocks.text: Different employers format this differently. But nearly every Canadian pay stub breaks down into the same five pieces.

items.title: Gross pay
items.text: What you earned before anything comes off.

items.title: CPP
items.text: Canada Pension Plan. Goes toward your retirement.

items.title: EI
items.text: Employment Insurance. Covers you if you lose your job or take certain leaves.

items.title: Income tax
items.text: Federal and provincial, combined into one line or split into two.

items.title: Net pay
items.text: What lands in your account.

blocks.text: That’s the whole shape. Now let’s take each one apart.

sections.title: CPP: the one that builds your future

blocks.text: CPP is not a savings account with your name on it. It is a public pension that you and your employer pay into together.

Your employer matches every dollar you pay. In return, you earn a monthly pension for life, which can start as early as age 60. The more years you pay in, and the more you earn, the bigger that pension gets. Nobody gets to opt out.
In 2026, you pay 5.95% of your earnings, but not all of them. The first $3,500 you earn each year is exempt. Above $74,600, this rate stops.
There is a second, smaller layer called CPP2. It applies only to earnings between $74,600 and $85,000, at a lower rate of 4%. Most people never reach it. Higher earners do.

Put together, the most anyone pays into CPP in 2026 is $4,646.45: $4,230.45 on the first layer and $416 on CPP2. After that, CPP stops coming off your pay for the rest of the year. You also get some of it back at tax time, as a credit and a deduction on your return.

items.title: “CPP is money the government keeps.”
items.text: CPP isn’t a pot of cash with your name on it, but it isn’t lost either. Every year you pay in builds your record, and that record sets the size of your pension. You can see your record in your My Service Canada Account. Quebec workers pay into the Quebec Pension Plan (QPP) instead, at slightly different rates.

sections.title: EI: the safety net you hope to never use

blocks.text: Employment Insurance is smaller than CPP. It’s simpler too.

You pay 1.63% of your earnings in 2026, up to a cap. Once you earn $68,900 in the year, EI stops. The most anyone pays is $1,123.07. Quebec workers pay a lower EI rate, plus premiums for the Quebec Parental Insurance Plan.
Your employer pays 1.4 times what you pay. That is their cost, not yours, but it’s worth knowing it exists.

What does EI buy you? Income support if you’re laid off. Paid time off during parental leave. Help during some illnesses and caregiving. You hope you never need it, but most workers use it at some point.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE YEAR YOU SWITCH JOBS, WATCH FOR THIS

CPP and EI both have yearly caps. Once you hit them, the deductions stop for the rest of the year. Here’s the catch: each employer tracks your earnings on its own. If you work two jobs, or switch jobs partway through the year, both employers may take CPP and EI from scratch, even if you had already maxed out at the old job. The good news: you get your extra share back as a credit when you file your tax return. The bad news: you won’t see it until then. A year with a job change can mean smaller paycheques now and a bigger refund later. Knowing that in advance means it won’t feel like a mistake.

sections.title: Income tax: the part everyone assumes is one flat cut

blocks.text: It isn’t. Canada’s income tax is layered, like a set of shelves.

Your first chunk of income is taxed at the lowest rate. The next chunk, a little higher. And so on, climbing as your income climbs. Only the part of your income sitting on a shelf pays that shelf’s rate.
For 2026, the federal shelves look like this. Up to $58,523, taxed at 14%. From there to $117,045, 20.5%. From there to $181,440, 26%. Then 29%, and 33% above $258,482.
Nobody pays 33% on their whole income. Only the slice above $258,482 gets that rate. Everything below still sits on its own, lower shelf.

On top of federal tax, your province adds its own shelves and rates. That’s why two people with the same salary in different provinces take home different amounts. The next lesson, Marginal Tax Rates, takes the whole system apart.

items.title: “A raise that bumps me into a higher bracket means I’ll take home less money.”
items.text: Moving into a higher bracket only means your next dollars are taxed at the higher rate. Every dollar you already earn keeps its old, lower rate, so your take-home pay still goes up. One thing can shrink the gain: benefits based on income, like the Canada Child Benefit or the GST/HST credit, get a little smaller as income rises. You still come out ahead, just by less than the raise alone suggests.

sections.title: The slice of your income that’s never taxed at all

blocks.text: Before any of those shelves apply, there’s a floor.
It’s called the Basic Personal Amount. In 2026, it’s $16,452 federally. Think of it as the first stretch of your income that gets a free pass: no federal tax touches it.

Almost everyone gets the full amount. People earning over about $181,000 get a slightly smaller one, down to $14,829. It’s built into your paycheque deductions automatically, so you don’t need to apply for it.
Your province has its own version too, at its own amount.
Your 2026 deductions at a glance

items.title: CPP (first layer)
items.text: 5.95% — on earnings from $3,500 to $74,600. The most you pay is $4,230.45.

items.title: CPP2
items.text: 4% — on earnings from $74,600 to $85,000. The most you pay is $416.

items.title: EI
items.text: 1.63% — on earnings up to $68,900. The most you pay is $1,123.07.

items.title: Federal income tax
items.text: 14% to 33% — layered by shelf, with no yearly cap. Your province adds its own.

items.title: I can find gross pay, and I know it’s the starting number, not the final one.
I can find CPP and EI as two separate lines, not one combined deduction.
I know whether my income tax line is federal only, or federal and provincial combined.
I know roughly where I sit on the federal tax shelves this year.
I know if I’ve changed jobs this year, since that can mean CPP and EI restart from zero.
I know net pay is what’s left after all of the above, not a separate deduction itself.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: WHY YOUR FIRST PAYCHEQUE OF THE YEAR LOOKS DIFFERENT

Notice your take-home pay creeping up late in the year, with no raise? That’s CPP or EI hitting its yearly cap. Once you’ve paid the most for the year, that line drops off your stub until January resets it. It works the other way too. Your first paycheque each January can look smaller than December’s, at the same salary, because CPP and EI start fresh. Neither is an error. Both are the caps doing their job.
Devon’s first real paycheque
paragraphs: Devon got his first full-time job offer at twenty-three: $48,000 a year, working for a building supply company in Edmonton. On the drive home he did the math in his head. Forty-eight thousand dollars, split into twenty-six paydays, came to about $1,846 every two weeks. That night he picked out an apartment based on that number.
Two weeks later, his first deposit landed, and it was a few hundred dollars short of $1,846. Devon stared at his banking app in disbelief. Payroll had messed up. It had to be.

He typed an angry email to HR and hovered over Send. Then he stopped, because if he was wrong, that email would be the first thing his new boss knew about him. He saved it as a draft and texted his friend Amira, who worked in accounting.

“Read me the lines on your stub,” she wrote back. He went through them one at a time: gross pay, CPP, EI, federal tax, Alberta tax and net pay. Amira explained each line in under five minutes, and every number was right.

Then came the part he didn’t expect. Amira told him the CPP line wasn’t money he had lost. It was building his own pension, and his employer was paying the same amount on top. She showed him how to check his record in his My Service Canada Account. The line that had annoyed him most was the one working hardest for him.

Devon deleted the draft. He redid his budget on paper, this time using his real net pay, and chose a cheaper apartment. Now, every payday, he does the math with the stub in front of him, not in his head on the drive home.

blocks.text: Your stub breaks into five pieces: gross pay, CPP, EI, income tax and net pay. CPP and EI both stop once you hit a yearly cap. Income tax is layered, not flat, so a raise never shrinks your take-home pay. A job change partway through the year can mean CPP and EI restart, and that evens out at tax time.
Budget from your real pay, and every payday stops being a surprise.
blocks.detail: When you know what comes off and why, you can plan around your net pay and catch a payroll mistake early.

blocks.text: Worksheet: decode your own stub

Answer guidance: if your stub shows CPP and EI as one combined number, ask payroll to split it. You’re entitled to see both. If your tax line is unclear, check the fine print or ask HR. If your net pay doesn’t match your deposit, look for other small deductions like union dues, pension plan or benefit premiums. Those sit outside this lesson’s five lines.

items.title: Gross pay
items.text: What you earned, before any deductions.

items.title: Net pay
items.text: What lands in your account, after every deduction.

items.title: CPP
items.text: Canada Pension Plan. A public pension you and your employer pay into, which pays you a monthly pension later.

items.title: CPP2
items.text: A second, smaller CPP layer on earnings between two set limits.

items.title: EI
items.text: Employment Insurance. Covers job loss, parental leave, and some illness or caregiving leave.

items.title: Basic Personal Amount
items.text: The slice of income that is never taxed federally.

items.title: Tax bracket
items.text: A range of income taxed at one specific rate. Higher brackets apply only to the income above them.

blocks.text: Educational only, not tax advice. Figures shown are 2026 federal rates. Confirm your own province and year before relying on any number here.
